messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya is a 19-year-old dancer who lives alone in a small apartment near the studio where she trains six days a week. Nine months ago, she was caught in a mass shooting at a crowded outdoor festival. She had gone with friends to see a headliner, but when the gunfire started, the crowd surged and she was knocked to the ground. For what felt like an eternity, she lay pinned beneath strangers, unable to move, her face pressed into the dirt, the acrid smell of smoke and cordite filling her lungs. She remembers the weight of bodies on her back, the screams, and the terrifying certainty that she was going to die. She eventually crawled free, but the memory has never loosened its grip.

When Maya thinks about that night, the memory returns with a horrifying sensory completeness. She can smell the smoke and the sharp, metallic tang of blood as if she were still lying on the ground, and the physical sensation of being crushed and restrained is so vivid that she sometimes gasps and tries to push the air away with her hands. Yet when she tries to describe what happened to her therapist, she finds herself unable to find the words—the experience feels too vast and formless to put into language, and she sits in silence, shaking her head. She has come to believe that if she lets herself think about the event in any detail, she will not be able to handle it, and this belief has led her to actively avoid her own memories. She is also haunted by a deep sense of injustice; she watches news reports of the investigation stalling, and she feels that what happened to her was profoundly unfair and that nothing has been done about it. This belief fuels her avoidance: she tells herself there is no point in talking about it because no one will make it right.

In the months after the shooting, Maya began to notice changes in how she moved through the world. She started avoiding going out, especially at night, and she gave up the pleasant activities she used to enjoy—meeting friends for coffee, browsing at the weekend market. She found herself covering her face with her hands whenever she walked past a police car or heard a siren, a reflexive gesture she could not explain. These strategies, however, have only made things worse. The more she stays home, the more exhausted she feels, and that exhaustion itself becomes a trigger: when she is tired, her guard drops and the memory surges back with full sensory force. She now wakes during the night to check whether she is safe, scanning the dark room before she can fall back asleep. During the day, she has difficulty concentrating; in dance class, she loses her place in the choreography, and her instructor has noticed. She has also become hypervigilant to unexpected movement—when another dancer rushes past her in the studio, she flinches hard, her heart pounding, as if the danger is still present. This constant state of alertness leaves her drained, and the fatigue then loops back, making her more vulnerable to intrusive memories and to feeling followed or tracked when she is alone on the street. She is certain she is being watched, even when no one is there.

Maya’s daily environment as a dancer has become a minefield. The physical contact required in partnering work—being held, lifted, or restrained in a pose—can suddenly trigger the tactile sensation of being pinned down, and she will freeze, her face hidden in her hands. She has started arriving late to rehearsals to avoid the crowded changing room, and she has stopped going out with the company after performances. Her social life has narrowed to almost nothing. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in class last week when she dropped to the floor, covering her head, unable to breathe, after a fellow dancer accidentally bumped into her from behind. Her teacher pulled her aside and told her she could not continue like this. Maya is terrified that the memory will never fade, and she is desperate to find a way back to the person she was before—the dancer who moved freely, without checking every shadow.
